To my knowledge, the majority of the men worked about two months in the forestry conservation camps. They were paid thirty cents an hour, and they paid seventy-five cents a day for board while in the camps. On May 17 Mr. Pearson, minister of labour for British Columbia, made a public statement in these terms:
During the winter season of 1937-38 the provincial government in cooperation with the dominion government, have provided relief through our forest development plan to 1,800 single homeless men who were recent arrivals from other provinces and in the province before November 1, 1937.
We believe that during the summer months it is possible for these single men who are our own residents to find sufficient work to provide for themselves during the summer and in many cases also during the winter, but the added burden of the accumulation from other provinces makes it difficult for our own residents to get the work that is available.
The province of British Columbia does not intend to make provincial forest development projects available to those from outside the province next winter, nor to provide any other form of assistance for them.
We feel that it is desirable that the 1,800 men who have been supported in this province during the past winter in forest development projects should return to the province from which they came as rapidly as possible.

In order to make this possible the provincial government will assist those men to return to the province of previous residence, and it is requested that these men make application to 581 Homer street, Vancouver, for such assistance.

dominion contributed.

made a contribution. I am referring to what the minister read just now.

speechtext:
We did contribute fifty
per cent of the cost of these forestry conservation camps, and we did so to meet a peculiar situation, namely, a flow of transients from the prairies to British Columbia during the winter months. Hon. members who are familiar with the climate of British Columbia can readily understand why the movement should be in that direction in the winter months. The farm employment plan which dealt with single, homeless men in the prairie provinces was not applicable in British Columbia, and, therefore, that province asked us as a dominion government to cooperate with them in providing these special forestry conservation projects for single, homeless men in the winter months. It was not an innovation to close these camps at the end of the winter season. That course had been followed in the previous year without any untoward incident. Actually the farm employment plan in the prairie provinces was terminated at the same time, and advance notice was given of the intention of the governments concerned to bring this plan to an end at the end of April of this year.
The statement has been made that the majority of the men concerned in the Vancouver incident were non-residents. The report of Mr. Pearson of May 17 states that there were 1,800 non-resident transients in the forestry conservation camps during the winter months. The actual number at the closing of the camps is known. As I remember, it was close to 1,500, and we know that over 800 of the deferred pay vouchers were cashed outside British Columbia. That would leave a total of somewhere in the neighbourhood of 700 non-residents who were in Vancouver at the time the post office was occupied originally.
Just a few days ago the youth council of the city of Vancouver made a survey of the men who were actually in occupation of the art gallery and the post office in order to determine how many were non-residents and how many were single, unemployed men properly resident in British Columbia. Fol-
lowing that survey, which was made public, Mr. Pearson made the following statement:
Statement of youth council confirmed views of government in regard to its stand on sit down strike in Vancouver. Strike started with sixteen hundred transients participating and now according to the youth council survey there are only one hundred of the originals. Thus fifteen hundred transients have left and have apparently found the means of livelihood.
Some members of this house may have seen the report of the survey being conducted by the youth council. It showed clearly that of those who took part in the demonstrations in the art gallery and the post office not more than 100 could be described as non-resident.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE-VANCOUVER SITUATION
speechtext: Is the minister basing his statement entirely on the survey that was made?

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE-VANCOUVER SITUATION
speechtext:
That is the only information we have as to those who were in occupation of the art gallery and the post office. The government has no reason to believe that the facts are not as stated, nor do I have any reason to assume that the youth council would have any motive in stating the facts other than correctly.
Why is it that this house should now be discussing this matter upon the motion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that we should give our attention to a question of urgent public importance? What has altered the situation is the fact that on Sunday morning the men who were in occupation of the art gallery and post office were asked to vacate these buildings. Having refused to do so, they were evicted by the city police. At the post office the city police had the cooperation of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. What is the proximate cause of the riot that occurred in Vancouver? The proximate cause surely is this, that these men who were asked to withdraw peaceably, and who were given thirty minutes to do so, declined to comply with that request, made in one case by the postmaster and in the other by the secretary of the board of trustees of the art gallery. Had they complied with that request; had they taken advantage of the time given, there would have been no riots; no injuries would have been suffered by policemen and men, and there would have been no destruction of private property. What did occur was the result of the fact that when asked to leave these buildings the men refused to do so.
Had those men complied with that request which was made after great patience and forbearance so far as the maintenance of law and order was concerned, would their position have been any different from that of other

Unemployment-Vancouver Situation
groups of unemployed in cities and towns right across this dominion? I put that directly to members of this house. Had these men accepted the advice given, they would have been in precisely the same position as other groups of unemployed in other towns and cities with respect to available employment. They would not have suffered discrimination.

Perhaps my hon. friend
will permit me to finish. I am not aware that I interrupted him in his rather vehement discourse this afternoon. A short while ago I met a delegation of unemployed from the city of Charlottetown, at the other extremity of this dominion. It so happens that the little province of Prince Edward Island has suffered from rather exceptional weather conditions during the past year. To-day there is a greater number of unemployed in Charlottetown than they have had at any time in the past ten years. So they appealed to us. This delegation from Charlottetown was composed of men some of whom were unemployed themselves. They put their case before us, and I told them, as my predecessors have told similar delegations in times past, that the government had made certain appropriations for relief and for public works and that within those appropriations we would do what we could to meet the situation in the city of Charlottetown. Those men set out certain projects which they thought would help particularly to meet the situation, and they left their information with me. It has been found possible to proceed with some of those, but it will not be possible to proceed with others.
The point I wish to make is this: Those men made their proposals and then accepted the decision that the government was prepared to do certain things, but was not prepared to carry out all their requests. They went back to Charlottetown and made their report to the unemployed of that city. The unemployed of that city did not occupy the post office or any other public building. They recognized the fact that any government with a sense of its responsibilities can do much in certain directions, but cannot, and least of all under dictation, provide special works projects for special groups of people in special districts in this dominion. I suggest that in effect that was the purpose of this organized demonstration in Vancouver.
You will find nothing in the correspondence exchanged between the Minister of Labour and the head of the unemployed committee which could by any stretch of the imagination be described as provocative. From the 51952-256
beginning I have been willing to concede that these men were honestly desirous of obtaining work. I pointed out to Mr. Matts of the unemployed committee that these men could not expect and need not expect that this government would provide special works projects for this particular group of people. I believe that position was sound then and I believe it is no less sound now. Despite the fact that these men, under ill advice, have chosen illegal methods to bring their plight to the attention of the government, there has been no desire on the part of the government to discriminate against them. At the present time these men stand on the same footing as other unemployed in British Columbia or in other provinces to which they may have gone. Surely it cannot be argued for a moment that we should provide special works projects for a group of men who have adopted the methods these men have adopted and decline to provide special works projects for the unemployed of Charlottetown and other places who have gone about their business in an entirely proper and legal way.

As I said at the beginning, I think it is fortunate that this matter has been discussed in temperate language and that there has been no resort to harsh and bitter words. Looking to the future, I can only say that we, with the other governments concerned, will do what lies in our power to see that employment is made available to these men on the same terms as it is made available to others who are in the same position. More cannot be said; and less, I think, cannot justly be said.
As a matter of fact, only a few days ago Premier Pattullo gave a full statement, which appeared in the Vancouver papers, of the public work that will be available in British Columbia during the coming summer. Some two weeks before that, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) made a statement with regard to special work which would be conducted through federal contributions. The total amount of public works in British Columbia in the way of highway construction will be in the neighbourhood of two and a half million dollars, quite apart from other public expenditures which will be made by various departments of government; nor does that at all cover such work as .may be made available through private enterprise. Some have said here to-day it is not reasonable to expect that any work

will be made available through the expansion of private enterprise. Our figures show that there were 15,000 placements made through the employment service in British Columbia last year, which surely suggests that in the course of the summer months opportunities for employment are made available from time to time. And I am convinced it is far from the truth to say that you can judge as to the employment possibilities in British Columbia or any other province only by a recital of the public works which are either actually under construction or in contemplation. In this country we have never depended upon public works as the sole means of providing employment, and I think it is a mistake to base any of our discussions upon such an assumption. Public works have their place in an employment policy, and we have tried to give them their proper place. As a government we have continued to do what we could to expand employment opportunities in British Columbia and elsewhere.
These men who unfortunately, under wrong advice, took part in this demonstration in Vancouver which had such an unhappy ending should think carefully before they lend themselves to this means of bringing their position before governments. I have every sympathy for their position; so has every member of this house, irrespective of party; but I do suggest that it is not proper for one group of unemployed in one section of the country to take the position that they will occupy public buildings until given special works projects in that section of the country. No government, I submit, whatever its character might be, could accept dictation of that kind. Before I close, however, I should like to make it equally clear that despite what has happened this government will not lend itself to any discrimination against these men. What I said two weeks ago I repeat with equal force now. These men will be upon the same footing as others in similar groups of unemployed, either in British Columbia or in other provinces.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon my
mind goes back three years, to the time when into the city of Regina there came a group of young men, also from British Columbia. I remember how gentlemen now sitting on the opposite side of the house then took an attitude somewhat different from that taken by hon. gentlemen sitting on that side of the house this afternoon, and I listened with a great deal of interest to the defence of the government policy offered by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers).
May I deal with just one or two things the Minister of Labour said. He told us that the men were employed during the winter months and that they had certain vouchers coming to them which should have enabled them to maintain themselves for a considerable time. That, at least, is the inference I took from his remarks. Apparently they worked for eight weeks, and there was a deferred payment of $4 a week. That would amount to a maximum of $32, with which not only to provide food and shelter but to buy clothing to maintain themselves until they could get a problematical job. I say, "a problematical job" because, as has been shown in the house this afternoon and on other occasions recently, in British Columbia men are being laid off instead of taken on, and the situation in that regard becomes more serious every day.

Unemployment-Vancouver Situation
We also have the question of whether these men are from within or without that province, and we are told that a survey by the youth council showed that seventy-five per cent of these men were residents of British Columbia. At this point may I just interject a question as to why the minister has relied upon a survey made by the youth council when there was an officer of his department in Vancouver and when, if my recollection is correct, it was suggested some days ago from this corner of the house that this officer or other officers of the department should make an official survey of unemployed young men in Vancouver. Why should we have quoted to us figures that are unofficial when we might have had before us this afternoon an official statement?
We are told that it is not an innovation to close the winter camps, because they were closed last year and the men were sent out to look for jobs themselves. That is quite true, but the condition last year was entirely different from the condition that exists this year. Last year there was employment; this year men are being laid off, and unemployment in British Columbia is increasing. That explains the difference in conditions, and why the men found it necessary to bring their case as forcibly as possible, without doing violence, before the government and the people of Canada generally. We are told that the men were asked to vacate the premises and refused to do so. We have not been told that they were offered any real alternative. They were not offered food; they were not offered shelter elsewhere. I would not at any time encourage a trespass; but after all if a trespass is going to 'be committed, I would say that the place to trespass would be upon public property rather than the property of private citizens and individuals. These buildings were public institutions, and therefore to that extent the men showed a considerable amount of judgment in occupying what was public property. We are told they were evicted by the city police, in cooperation with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. That point has been emphasized this afternoon. I wonder if it is not a similar situation to that which existed in Regina in 1935 when, more or less unwillingly, the city police were compelled to take the first step in the regrettable riot which occurred on the market square. If my information is correct, the mounted police officers were in reality directing the operation, and the city chief of police was more or less acting under instruction from the federal authorities. If that be so, I think we should know about it.

We are told that had the men complied there would have been no riot, no injury and no destruction of property. But would there have been any shelter? Would there have been any food? Would any work have been provided by the government for these men? I think these are important questions.
We are told that they could have done what other young men in other parts of Canada are doing. When I came back from Saskatchewan the other day I travelled over the Canadian National road. It is probable that other hon. members who were in Saskatchewan may have travelled over the same route, and if they did they would have noticed little jungles at stations all along the way where little groups of men were congregated trying to cook their food over improvised fires. Is that the sort of thing to which the government would sentence our young men, day in and day out, week in and week out?
I say the time has come when we must view the situation as something more than a passing phase. As the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) said this afternoon, the technological improvements made in industry in the last few years have created

an entirely ne,w situation, one which must be grappled with. It seems to me that in allowing the condition to drift, the government is simply inviting trouble for itself and for the entire dominion. Any one who knows me must know that I have no use for violence. Whenever I have had the opportunity I have endeavoured to advise means of protest which were other than provocative of violence. One. of the members of the group to which I belong was responsible, so I am informed, for preventing a far more serious situation from developing at Vancouver yesterday. That has been our point of view. Consequently, when we bring these matters to the attention of the house we do so in the interests of peace, order and good government.
We have heard about a difference in the attitude of men from Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island. I do not know anything about those men, but I do know that conditions in New Brunswick are none too good. There has been no relief for a considerable time. However, if the people in New Brunswick are prepared to accept conditions such as no respectable Canadian ought to accept, then of course that is the business of the people of New Brunswick. And if the people in other parts of Canada-

Mr. Speaker, this afternoon we of the group with which I am associated were asked what alternatives we had to offer. For three years now we, in common with other members of the house, have been bringing to the attention of parliament this grave problem of unemployment. Always we have tried to make constructive proposals, and now towards the end of the third session of this parliament all that the government seems to have done is to have achieved a near approach to a balanced budget, and tear gas bombs for the unemployed at Vancouver. May I say that in my opinion along that path lies revolution, and that is not the alternative which we suggest. Our alternative is to recognize that within the present economic system with its technological dislocation, and so on, there is no cure; but that pending the changes which must come, work and wages must be provided by governments for our unemployed, and more particularly perhaps for our young people. The national employment commission warned the government, and its chairman, Mr. Purvis, stated, as reported in the Montreal Gazette of January 12, 1937:
Sometimes it is assumed that the good times for which we look so hopefully will automatically take care of all dangers inherent in the relief and unemployment situations. The commission does not believe this to be the case.
Nor, may I add, will one good crop or two good crops in the west cure the disease. It is time we realized it is a disease, and a disease of the present economic system. Unless we take steps to cure it, it is, I believe, the cancer that will destroy the system and perhaps even civilization itself. Obviously only employment will cure unemployment, and I submit, everywhere in this country there is work to be done.
This afternoon I spoke of my recent trip to Saskatchewan and what I saw upon my return over the Canadian National railway.

Unemployment-Vancouver Situation
I went west over the Canadian Pacific railway, and I could not help noticing, as we passed through western Ontario and along the shores of the great lakes, the miles and miles of half-completed trans-Canada highway. The completion of that highway alone would mean work, plenty of work, and wages too. If, Mr. Speaker, you had travelled, as I did, over the Saskatchewan roads, you would have realized that there was a great deal of work to be done in that province, as well as in the other provinces. Quite recently, a few Sundays ago, I was on a train coming out of Montreal. We struck an automobile, and a priest and his driver were killed. I noted that during the same week the press of this city reported three fatal automobile accidents at level crossings quite near to the city of Montreal; yet I remember that the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) before the election of 1935 spoke of the dangers of level crossings and the necessity of eliminating them, and incidentally he spoke of their elimination as one of the possibilities of finding employment for those persons then unemployed. I say, too, that in the elimination of level crossings there is work to be done, work that would provide wages for many unemployed. Reforestation, afforestation, drought control-

speechtext:
I would draw the attention of the hon. member to the fact that the motion now under discussion deals "with the serious situation existing in Vancouver as a result of the eviction of single unemployed men from the post office, and at once to stop disturbances." I would ask the hon. member to confine his remarks as closely as possible to the subject.
' Mr. COLD WELL: May I draw the attention of Your Honour to the fact that in the debate before the supper recess we were asked what alternatives we had to suggest to relieve the unemployment situation among transients at Vancouver, and I am endeavouring to show that there are alternatives to tear gas bombs and so on, by pointing out that there is much work with wages to be done in the Dominion of Canada. But if your honour considers that I am out of order, I shall confine my remarks more specifically to the Vancouver situation.
In regard to the unemployed at Vancouver it should be said that in order that they may provide themselves with food, clothing and shelter they require money, and it has been said also that public works projects cannot be financed either in British Columbia or elsewhere because we cannot finance them. I would point this out, that there is a tremendous waste to-day in the investment of
money-exaggerated speculation, bad investments, uncontrolled investment, the putting of money into unproductive and speculative channels and so on. Thus I believe, if the government would parallel the recent announcement that it would nationalize the Bank of Canada in order to give greater control of currency and credit, with an announcement that it would establish a national investment board, money could be found to provide for many work and wages programs.
Retirement of the aged from industry, provision for minimum wages and shorter hours are other alternatives that might be suggested. But again I would ask of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers): What are these transients who have been treated in this manner in the city of Vancouver to do at the present, time? Where to-day can a single unemployed man or woman get a meal, a bed, or necessary clothing? What are the single unemployed residents of the city of Vancouver itself to do? These are questions to which the house is entitled to an answer at the present time, and I submit that we have had no answer, and that before this debate ends the government should give parliament the assurance that unemployment conditions at the coast and elsewhere will be met at once.
We were asked what alternatives we had. I have submitted some which we have brought to the attention of this house from time to time since we assembled in February, 1936; but, after all, it is not our function to suggest a program or a policy to the government, for the government now in power promised in 1935 to cure, or at least to alleviate, unemployment so that it would not be the great problem it is to-day. The government accepted office upon the conditions which the government itself laid down to the people of Canada. The government has the power to fulfil its promises; for no other government in Canadian history ever had the following which this government has in this House of Commons. We have told the house from time to time what we advise. That is all we can do.
Again I ask. What does the government propose to do? Out of office the present Prime Minister was loud in his expressions of horror at tne condition that then existed, a condition wkfjsMis closely paralleled by the conditio!? at Vancouver and in other parts of Canada to-day and only this afternoon the Prime Minister expressed satisfaction over an improvement in conditions. But for whom have conditions improved? Not for the thousands of young men who ride the rods all across Canada; not for the thousands of young men and young women who are leaving our schools and our colleges
4044	COMMONS
Unemployment-Vancouver Situation
every year without any prospects in life; not for the masses of the people because unemployment and insecurity haunt this whole land from coast to coast. Our young people, thousands of them, are idle. They cannot establish homes or lead decent, normal lives, and I submit that tear gas bombs are no answer to this question.
And so, Mr. Speaker, before I sit down I should like again to ask the Minister of Labour what he proposes to do in regard to these conditions. We have not heard; we have not been informed. All that we have been told is that these young men can do the same thing as other young people are doing throughout this dominion. Having in some degree at least answered the question which government spokesmen asked of this little group to-day, I ask the government: What is your alternative?

It is regrettable that there was so little of hope in the statement made this afternoon by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers), and no indication whatever that the government is facing this situation. I do not know what will happen if the government continues its ostrich-like policy of burying its head in the sand whenever trouble of this kind looms on the horizon. The British Columbia government deserves, it seems to me, just as much censure as the dominion government. It too has failed utterly to face the problem. Today we find in the Ottawa papers this report from Victoria:
Honourable George Pearson, Minister of Labour, refused to meet a delegation of Vancouver unemployed who came here to-day.
That is no way to tackle the problem. One reason why the government here is falling down is that it is trying to settle the problem by remote control. Ottawa is three thousand miles away from Vancouver. It is true that this government has a representative in Vancouver, but his efforts appear to have been worthless. Some weeks ago I suggested that the Minister of Labour should go to Vancouver and personally take charge of the situation there before it became impossible, but no move was made. It is just like a colonel trying t^^fight his battalion without ever having a lOTfc at the front line. The place of the federal' Minister of Labour is at the present time in Vancouver, and the sooner he gets there the faster this problem will be solved. His absence is a continuation of the policy which apparently has been adopted by this government. I believe only one front-bench minister has been in British Columbia since the election three years ago.
IMr. Coldwell.]
That was the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar). They have all been too busy.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE-VANCOUVER SITUATION
speechtext:
In the course of his remarks this afternoon the minister said that the cause of yesterday's trouble was that the men had refused to leave the building peaceably when requested to do so. But the trouble goes far deeper than that. The real cause of this trouble in Vancouver at the present time is the failure of the dominion government to face the problem of the single transient unemployed, which centres in Vancouver. Each spring and each fall these single unemployed, who have no home attachments drift out to Vancouver. It is the end of the two great railway lines. The weather is milder than it is in the east, not so cold in the winter and not so hot in the summer-fortunately. The government forestry camps in British Columbia are closed each spring. There is not the opportunity for the men from those camps to get work in the forest industries of our province, such as there is for men on the farms to carry on with farm work during the summer. The problem is in Vancouver, not in Charlottetown, and it has been in Vancouver year after year. This is no new thing. Plainly it is the responsibility of the dominion government, not of the citizens of Vancouver. In that city, according to another press dispatch, ten thousand people congregated this morning at the Canadian Pacific Railway docks to see this delegation of one hundred off to Victoria to interview the provincial minister of labour. You have no idea of the effect that has on the citizens of Vancouver and on the business of the city, of the effect that the fact of these hundreds of men being parked in the public buildings has had in lowering the morale of the whole of our citizenry. It has affected seriously the business of Vancouver; it has ruined the summer so far as that great city is concerned; tourist business has been very badly hurt; business in all other lines is

Unemployment-Vancouver Situation
suffering. There is no reason why the citizens of Vancouver or any other city should have to pay the shot because of the failure of governments to tackle this problem of the single transient unemployed.
Time and again during the last two months we have pointed out to the government that there was going to be trouble and have advocated steps which could be taken to stop it. The only thing we have had from this government was the statement by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) this afternoon that the government is very sorry that this has happened. I believe that before they are through with their term of office they will be sorry for many more of their sins of omission, of which this is one of the worst. The question is, What can be done now? These men are still in Vancouver. There is no possibility whatever of their being placed in industry, no possibility of their getting work for themselves. But public works projects are being undertaken in British Columbia, and several million dollars are to be spent. Also training is to be given in forestry and in placer mining. I suggest to the minister that all these unemployed men who are eligible for employment on public works, or for the training, should be registered forthwith; a record should be got of the men who can be put on these projects, and an assurance should be given that they will be placed in the next few days. There is no reason why some step of that kind cannot be taken. It may be that there will have to be further public works; but I suggest that the solution of the problem lies along that line, and that there should be included among the men eligible for this work the transients who were in British Columbia camps all winter. The minister will correct me if I am wrong, but I understand that if a man was in British Columbia before November 1 of last year he was eligible for the forest camps during the winter. Is that correct?

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE-VANCOUVER SITUATION
speechtext: That is correct.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE-VANCOUVER SITUATION
speechtext:
I suggest that men of that group should be given a chance to work in British Columbia this summer. Two years ago the government worked out a plan whereby thousands of young men found employment on the railway lines doing maintenance work. Why could not something of that kind be set up this year? The provinces are not responsible for these transients; they are the problem of the dominion, and sooner or later the dominion will have to evolve some scheme for dealing with them. For the transients as a whole, whom we have all seen riding the rods and living in these
jungles across Canada which have been referred to this afternoon, this government should provide some sort of training, in forestry, in mining, in agriculture or in fishing. The main point is that the single transient unemployed man is the problem of the dominion, and this problem must be faced without any further delay.

It is, I know, difficult to approach the consideration of this subject without either giving it a partisan aspect or being accused of doing so. But before I make any criticism of the situation I wish to dissociate myself entirely from the language used by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). He was thoroughly in his element along the line he pursued. He had not got into his stride before he brought in the textile industry, which is at least somewhat remote from the subject we are. discussing. A policy of attack, yes; a policy of tearing down, yes; but of building up we heard nothing. And that is not calculated to bring about what at least should be the ambition of all of us, namely, a peaceful settlement of this dreadful situation, which is a reproach to our city of Vancouver and to the province as well as to our dominion. As the hon. member who preceded me has said, it is highly calculated to do both the city and the province a great deal of harm in many ways.
Speaking on this subject some weeks ago, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) indicated that with the men working in the forestry conservation camps in the winter time and those taken care of by the farm placement plan there were some 5,000 men engaged in British Columbia, and that at the end of April or running on towards the middle of May they were more or less turned loose. As reported at page 3131 of Hansard he quoted the minister of labour of British Columbia as having said that, of that number, some 1,800 men were non-residents, outsiders, and that the province would undertake to take care of the remainder if they could get rid of the 1,800. Well, that was the initial error, or at any rate one of them. The minister was not informed of the situation when he made that statement, I am referring to the minister of labour of British Columbia. Apparently he is unaware of the change in conditions. A year ago his statement would have been true and the arrangement would have worked satisfactorily. But the conditions have changed, and changed materially. A good many of the logging camps have closed, and even the camps that have not closed are

Vnemployment-Vancouver Situation
affected by the low demand for their products, the result being that they are working on short time with abbreviated crews.
In the town of Port Alice in my constituency and in the town of Woodfibre in the constituency of the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil), both paper mills, manufacturing either pulp or paper, have entirely shut down and are unable to state when they anticipate opening up again. These two little towns involve 700 men who are thrown out of employment. Multiply that by four and you have nearly three thousand men, women and children in the shadow of relief, and these are only two instances. In the city of Powell River, represented by the hon. member for Vancouver North, the mills are not entirely closed down but have very considerably curtailed their output, and that has had its bearing upon my own district. It is the custom for them every year to let contracts for small logging outfits in the northern portion of the district I represent. They allot them a certain quantity and that provides a summer's work. When Powell River runs half time they do not want these other logs because they have enough in their own storage ponds, and this means that another lot of men are thrown out of employment. Some of these men have their homes in my district; but many of them come from Vancouver, and that is why I have an interest in the matter. It is therefore not possible, as the minister of labour of British Columbia said, to employ 5,000 extra men. That is one conspicuous mistake.
Again, there was hope of sending the men to the prairies; but the governments there, both provincial and municipal, said emphatically that they did not want the men and would not take them. The men naturally asked what was the use of trying to go there seeing that they would only be turned loose and asked to move in some other direction. Speaking on May 23 on this subject, I suggested to the government that there was a major job waiting for these men to do, work which they could well perform, in the building of a road on the west coast of Vancouver at a place between Hesquiat and Estevan Point. It is essential that a road be built there to afford facilities to get supplies to the wireless station, lighthouse and direction finding station. We have been fooling along for a number of years spending two or three thousand dollars every year and getting nowhere, whereas if we spent 130,000 and built a good road using relief labour we would be giving the men employment and, more than that, we would save the annual maintenance, because the maintenance of a road so constructed would be slight. As it is, we are patching the 'Mr. Neill.]
road here and there, patching up work that we did years ago. The construction of such a road as I suggest would have been work which these men, trained in the bush, would have been well fitted to perform.
We have heard a good deal about the character of these men. The term " red " has been used, but I suggest that they cannot be dismissed with a single condemnation of that kind. I notice that whenever any strike is successful it has invariably the sympathy of the local people, and where the local people are not in sympathy it is always a failure. I think it can be fairly said, at any rate those who read the press and who know the conditions will agree, that the people of Vancouver are sympathetic to these men. So far as the word " red " is concerned, I had an experience forty years ago which I cannot forget. I, too, was like these men in that same city and I did not know where my next meal was coming from. I knew what it was to be hungry. There was not relief nor were there any government supplies. What I wanted to mention, however, in connection with that experience, is the fact which I noted then, that the morale of the men deteriorated very rapidly. We did not use the word " morale " then; we spoke of the character of the men, and undoubtedly it deteriorated. I saw it in myself and in my chums. We had to eat to live, and even though we were striving zealously to get jobs, and odd jobs were secured from time to time, we got to the stage where we were almost afraid of getting a job, and we did not want to work. The less intelligent men might have become hoboes or petty thieves, and the more intelligent ones might have gone into some form of confidence game. I was seriously contemplating going into a scheme for smuggling Chinamen into the United States-a profitable occupation, with $500 a head profit and five years in the penitentiary if we were caught. We did not know the word "red" in those days; but if there had been any leadership there of any kind, that said, " We will show you the way out of this trouble," I certainly would have turned in that direction and so would my friends.
It is suggested that these men resorted to the action they did in order to force attention to their condition. Yes; and half the trouble in consequence is a matter of face saving on the part of both dominion and provincial governments and perhaps to some extent also on the part of the leadership of the men. The Minister of Labour said that in the winter months there was a conspiracy of which he had information. I have no doubt he knew what he was talking about. If there was not

Unemployment-Vancouver Situation
a conspiracy-that is going too far-there was at least a prearrangement that these men would be advised to get together in Vancouver when they were turned out of the camps, and so force the attention of the government to the situation with a view to getting the camps continued or to having work of some kind provided. And what was the conspiracy? One would expect to hear talk of Lenin's proposals and of taking from the rich and giving to the poor. But what, as a matter of fact, have these men asked for? So far as 1 can make out, all that they have demanded has been work. They said that they would be perfectly satisfied to get work, and they asked for the opening of a camp where they would work for a very small wage. It hardly looks, then, as if their sole motive were initiated by Moscow, when all they are asking for is the reopening of the labour camps.
And how was the situation handled? I do not think it was handled in the best way. The government positively encouraged, or any rate tacitly permitted it. In fact, more than that, they accepted it. They allowed food to go in and men to come out; they allowed for gangs to go out for baths, and arranged for baths. They went so far as to give them a sort of semi-valet service because they had their clothes fumigated. That is another mistake, because it constituted tacit approval.
I suggest that the proper way to do would have been to turn the men out at once; say to them, "You say you want to call attention to a grievance; well, you have called attention to it, and it will be investigated, on the good faith of the men who are sent to address you. But we will discuss no terms with revolutionists. Had a strong stand been taken, I think the men would have appreciated it. A committee could have been appointed, consisting of so many of these men, so many prominent citizens of Vancouver and so many government officials; let them sit down and discuss the subject. But apparently no attempt was made to come to an understanding. Let them agree on what I would call undeniable facts. For instance, the government said, "You can get lots of work on the prairies; go back there." But the men said, "We cannot get work there." The committee would then say, "There are two clear statements. We suggest it is up to the men to accept work that is offered them, and it is up to the government to state where they can find work"; not a mere statement that they will have their fare paid to Regina, whereupon the men will say, "What are we going to do when we get there?" and the government merely say, "Well, you will find out when you get there." Then, the
government having achieved the proper amount of face saving, a camp could have been opened. It will come to that anyway, and it does not make much difference in cost whether they are military or work camps. There would have been much less damage done either to the reputation of the government or to the shop windows of Vancouver than has taken place under the present system. The cost of opening that camp would have been small compared with the damage already done, and the situation is not eased one particle. I would tell these men, and tell them plainly, what was to be done; working men will stand to be told plain home truths; I have done it and received their approval.
Tell them that this is only a temporary arrangement. It seems to be at present largely a provincial issue, because if the Minister of Labour is correct, they are nearly all British Columbia residents now, although I think he is not quite right there; I think some of his figures did not take account of the fact that some men left and went back again. At any rate, if they are mostly our own residents, it is up to the provincial government, or the dominion government, to find work for them on the prairies or elsewhere. If there were a call for twenty teamsters, I would have twenty volunteers called up, and if twenty were not forthcoming I could conscript twenty whose occupations had been put down as such, and take them off relief. The bulk of the men would approve of that; they would not stand for shirkers, because their own interests are at stake. Or it could be done by provinces; say to Alberta: "We have fifty of your idle men. Will you provide for them and we will ship them to you, or will you pay for their work here?" I think one of the provinces did make such a suggestion, that they -would be willing to pay for maintenance in a camp in British Columbia. If the logging business or the paper industry picks up, as we all hope it will, there will be more employment along those lines, and it is wonderful how a slight increase in business will make the difference between too many men and too few. This may be called a mere dream of mine, but I think it is a practical and immediate solution; much more practical than talking about economic determinism, which is something I have never been able to understand and which I do not think is of any help in the present situation.
I have listened to the hon. members from Vancouver and vicinity talking about this matter at intervals for weeks now; they all spoke moderately and appropriately, and what did they get? They got just nowhere; they got language, beautiful language, and noth-

ing but language. I suppose I shall be called a rebel in saying this; but I am afraid if I had been one of that group or had a following on that side of the house, I should have been sorely tempted to follow the action of that great Liberal, I think it was Sir Wilfrid Laurier, in 1896, who said: "Not one more estimate shall pass until so-and-so happens." And on that occasion the matter in question was much less important than that before us to-night. If any considerable group on this side had said, "We will not pass another item in the estimates until this matter is settled," it would have been better for everyone. But surely such an attitude should not be necessary in these modern and supposedly enlightened days. The traditional policy of the Liberal party surely is still their policy- freedom of speech and protection and uplift of the masses. This is a great opportunity to carry out those principles. All that stands in the way is a little question of dignity; we have said this and we will not back down or give way one iota until they get out. Yes, we admit they were wrong; I think the men themselves will admit they were ten times wrong in the action they took. But there is a lurking suspicion that if they had not done something wrong, they would not have got any attention.
Let us put this matter above party political advantage. We are always appointing special committees. Let us suppose a committee of this house were appointed to-morrow, so many from the government side, so many from the Conservative party. I would put all the Vancouver members on it, but I would leave the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) off because he would make trouble in the Garden of Eden. But the various members from Vancouver who represent different parties and 'have shown a reasonable spirit should be on it; let that body get together, and I think they could speedily draw up a program which would bring this bitter matter to an end and do credit to every member and every party in this house.

The hon. member who last addressed us (Mr. Neill) very properly commented upon the immoderate language to which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) saw fit to treat the house in his presentation of his motion to-day. What is this all about? The hon. member to whom I last referred said that these men were not guilty of any crime. His next sentence was that the only crime they were guilty of is trespass. He has endeavoured throughout to make heroes of these unfortunate men who

through misguided leadership decided, as he puts it, to make a spectacular showing by breaking their country's laws. Do not let us forget that. Do not let us set up any false heroism; do not let us forget that these men have been guilty of taking over the property of His Majesty the King; and while I do not know enough about them to style them communists, I do know enough about the principles of communism to know that two things to which Stalin and communism are definitely opposed are constituted law and order. This is shown in taking forcible possession of public property and in denying art any place in society.
That leadership caused these men by mob rule to take forcible possession of the king's property, a post office, which has special significance under British law. It is a place where his majesty's mails are housed, where important communications pass back and forth. It is a place where the British flag flies at the masthead. The ill advisers of these unfortunate men led them to take forcible possession of his majesty's post office where the British flag ought to fly. It is all very well to say, "We must give them credit for their moderation in not beginning to break the windows in the post office." But the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre knows very well that the basic principle behind the policy these men adopted was mob rule and crowd psychology. In other words, they ganged up in order to take possession of one of his majesty's public buildings. What would the hon. gentleman think if a dozen or twenty men came along and said, "We are coming in here to sit down, to eat and sleep and perfume your place as we please." Suppose they came into his home or his garage or his stable, if he has one; what would he think of that, to bring it close to home in that way?
We know that in the country to the south we were treated to practically a year of sit-down strikes, and we know the battle the republic had to deal with them. We know what happened when they endeavoured to invade the province of Ontario, and these advisers of the unfortunate men in Vancouver are nothing more or less than sit-down strikers. The policy of the sit-down strikers is, "By our numbers we will change right into might. You dare not come near us." That was the defiance which was thrown out to Canada in Vancouver. The hon. gentleman, whose language I think I am not unfair in styling as incendiary and immoderate, called some of these men rascals, or said he expected some of them in the post office crowd were rascals.

We shall never make a great Canada if we have an admiration for the tearing down principle. If the hon. gentleman had enunciated a single cure or remedy for what he so glibly condemned, I might respect his address.
Let me say to the hon. member that in this country we need other things than a cavilling and political condemnation of men who are dealing with a difficult situation. We have been condemned because we did not start soon enough. To that extent, and that extent only, I agree with the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens). It would have been better had our friends taken what might have been regarded as a sterner, crueler course and ejected these men within the first twenty-four hours after they broke the law, if only as an example to the rest of Canada. I just wished to try to show how much real sincerity there was in all those fine words. In the first place, there is no use in talking about the problem confronting us in Vancouver unless we have some suggestion to offer for the solution of that 
problem. It has been said that all the men want is to get work and wages. In all the devices which the intelligence of man has thus far contrived, is there to be found any set of principles through which, if applied in Canada, these men could be given work and wages? If there is, then let us devote our attention to a discussion of those principles.
I was much pleased with the suggestion of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill). I am almost sure that the finest suggestion made thus far in the debate was made by that hon. member. I believe it was the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) who in his first speech this year suggested there must be enough intelligence and enough ideas in the house to solve our problems, if we all got together. This is the first time I have heard a re-echo of that fine suggestion.
The days through which we are passing present to Canada perhaps one of the first of the tragic effects of the break-down of the present system. I have quoted on former occasions some words which I believe will ring down through the generations, words of R. F. Irvine, Professor of Economics at Sydney university, Australia. For twenty-five years this man has been a professor of orthodox economics. Writing in 1933 in an article under the heading "Afterthoughts," he used the following words:
I believe the principles put forward by C. H. Douglas are not only sound but that they provide the only practical way of escape from the tragic fate which otherwise awaits the whole of western civilization.
If this man had been an ordinary farmer, an ordinary tradesman or an ordinary school teacher, his words might not have been very important. But he. is a professor of orthodox economics and for twenty-five years has been in one of the greatest universities in the British Empire. It was he who solemnly made those remarks. I believe they constitute a warning to this house. Out in Vancouver are manifestations of the tragic fate which otherwise awaits the whole of western civilization. That is the condition which will develop if we let that situation grow throughout the country, as I fear it will grow.
Much has been said about the other unemployed men who are quietly suffering. Either they are doing something about their lot, or they are simply suffering into the complete destruction of their bodies and souls. Let that condition continue, and we shall have a tragic fate all over this country; there is no doubt about that.

Therefore I am going to close what I have to say simply by pointing out that by changing to a system which is known to man today, known by hundreds of thousands of men, they can remove this blight which is threatening to destroy this people, and only by the adoption of some such plan as I have suggested to the house can it be done.
I am going to recall two fine statements made by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers).
1052	COMMONS
Unemployment-Vancouver Situation
Oae of them was this: "We will do what lies in our power." We suggest nothing but what lies in the government's power. There is control of Canada to-day by a government with a majority so great that it can do anything it chooses. If it cannot, then it would probably be quite in order for it to tell us why it cannot. If this country cannot govern itself, it is well that we should know it. If this parliament cannot govern this country, it is well that we should know it. If the present government with the majority it possesses cannot control this parliament, it is well that we should know it. If it can control this parliament, and this parliament can govern this country, and if this country can really govern itself, then it lies within the power of the government to-day to adopt the principles which I suggest. I contend they are the only solution.
The Minister of Labour also said this, as I remember it: "We will continue to do what we can to expand employment in British Columbia and elsewhere." Well, Mr. Speaker, all that the people of the Dominion of Canada request of the Minister of Labour and his colleagues is that they will do what they can. They need do no more.
I have no more to say. I shall not say anything unkind; I have not said anything unkind. All I shall do is to reiterate that the time has come for a show-down; the time has come for results, and the results will not be results of which this country can be anything but ashamed unless they give every man and every woman in this country at least a chance to make a living, a chance to get a job. Having said that, I just want to recall once more the words of R. F. Irvine. They are words to bear in mind. They are difficult words to laugh off.
I believe the principles put forward by C. H. Douglas are not only sound but that they provide the only practical way of escape from the tragic fate which otherwise awaits the whole of western civilization.
I commend to the Minister of Labour and to those who are charged with the responsibility of conducting this country through these trying years the application of the principles of Major C. II. Douglas.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext:
I have not my material here on this resolution, but I am familiar and I think the house is familiar with the object of it. The object is to precede the introduction of a bill authorizing the government to acquire by way of purchase all of the outstanding privately owned shares of the Bank of Canada and to convert the bank thereby into a wholly government owned as well as government controlled institution. The reason the government advances for this step is that during the past year it has become quite evident that there is to be not merely political controversy with respect to monetary policy generally, which of course is permissible and desirable, but political controversy relating to the constitution of the Bank of Canada, which is the chief instrument through which this parliament exercises its control over monetary policy in the country. The government is of opinion, after watching developments during the past two years, that it is highly undesirable and very much against the national interest that there should be continued political controversy with respect to the constitution of the bank itself. It is 51952-257
for that reason that, in addition to maintaining the control which the government now has through a substantial majority on the board of directors, the government should acquire the whole of the ownership of the shares of the bank. This has been suggested on more than one occasion by members on all sides of the house, and the government hopes that it will dispose once and for all of political discussion relating to the constitution of the bank itself.
There is, of course, no intention nor any hope that it will dispose of political discussion regarding the use which shall be made from time to time of this instrument of national control of monetary policy. I should say in this regard, however, that it is not the intention of the government by the introduction of this measure to make the Bank of Canada merely a department of government. If the central bank of a country is to serve the high purpose for which it is created, it must be manned by men who not only are expert in monetary, economic and financial matters, but also have a sufficient independence of judgment to be able at all times to talk on equal terms to the government of the day with respect to the matters which come under the jurisdiction of the bank in the ordinary course of business. It is not the intention that by this resolution the Bank of Canada should become in any way a political arm of government. That, indeed, would be fatal to the successful operation of the control of monetary policy and credit in this country.
I think, Mr. Chairman, that is all I can say at the moment, not having before me my material with respect to the matter, as to the intention of the government from the standpoint of policy in introducing this change.
As the Prime Minister announced some weeks ago, the price to be paid for the shares is the average price at which sales have been effected of the shares of the bank from the first of January this year to the date when be made the announcement in this house as to the policy of the government. The bill itself will deal with the details of the transfer, and I think that is all that I need say at this stage in order to secure the introduction of the bill.

speechtext:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: I do not think I can go further than I have gone. It was quite evident to the government during the last two years that the constitution of the bank was becoming and would likely continue to be a matter of political controversy. Doubt has been and is being cast upon the control of the bank by the government through a majority of the board of directors. This doubt it is proposed to remove altogether by purchasing the privately owned stock entirely, so that the people of Canada may know beyond per-adventure that the whole of their national central bank is owned by the government of Canada. That is the object. I believe it to be distinctly to the national advantage that there should not be continual political discussion regarding the constitution of the bank, but that discussion should be confined to the manner in which parliament decides that control shall be exercised through the instrument which we have in the central bank. I cannot add to that.

speechtext: I fancy that in the records of our parliament in recent years one would find it much more difficult to reconcile the speeches of the Minister of Finance in 1936 with this resolution than to find consistency on almost anything else with which we have had to deal. The only method by which we could make this a properly controlled bank was to have it controlled through the directorate, and the only means whereby that could be effected was to secure a larger number of directors than those originally suggested in the resolution. That was only a short time ago, and I venture to say that there has been less discussion publicly of the Bank of Canada in the last eighteen months than at any other time in its history. In the last twelve months there has been practically none at all. During 1935 there was a great deal of discussion on this subject initiated to a considerable extent by those now on the treasury benches, but in recent months there has been very little discussion about it. The public generally accepted the statement of the Minister of Finance that the method adopted, namely, of creating 85,100,000 worth of new stock and issuing it to the government was the most effective way to secure control.

It then becomes a political bank, which is the one thing one did endeavour to prevent. I am bound to say I appreciate the point of this bank being publicly owned. There was nothing said this afternoon or at any other time which was not presented to us; some of my colleagues at that time held very strong opinions, the matter was canvassed from every angle to try to arrive at a reasonable and fair understanding of the whole problem. The experience of other countries with central banks, some privately owned, some half owned by the public, some with a majority owned by the nation and some wholly owned by the public, as, for example, the Bank of England, was examined. After mature consideration, having regard to the pressure which was everywhere apparent, the conclusion that I have indicated was arrived at.
I have no view one way or the other as far as the general principle is concerned. I approached the problem of the creation of a central bank as a bank in which the stock would be owned by the nation; I abandoned it for reasons which I found it difficult to agree to in my own mind but from which I saw no escape, and ultimately my colleagues and I all agreed that this was the only way to prevent it from becoming a political bank. The history of some European countries with a publicly owned institution has been most distressing. I would hesitate to think Shat history could ever be repeated in this 'Country. But stripped of everything, this ibank now becomes a political bank; the directors are named by the government of the day. From that standpoint it is purely political.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC

What I endeavoured to say was that I was not wedded to the opposite idea. I said it in this chamber and said it publicly. I say still that is exactly the state of mind I was in at the time, and those are the reasons why the steps that were taken were taken.
But the government having decided to do this, naturally a great deal depends on the bill itself. The minister has said, quite correctly, that if this is to become a department of government, the usefulness of the Bank of Canada is largely gone. On the other hand, if it is to be an arm of government, its value still remains. There is a very great difference between being an arm of government and merely a department of government, and the distinction between the two will determine the value of this institution. Frankly I was amazed when the statement was made by the Prime Minister; for I think it has been generally considered that the bank has functioned fairly well; there has been an acceptance of it by the public generally as being useful, and to no inconsiderable extent it has justified the expectations of its friends. In one matter

Bank oj Canada
it undoubtedly had a great advantage over most such institutions, because it assumed the entire responsibility for our note issue.
Having assumed responsibility for our note issue, it always had in its exchequer three per cent on the outstanding note liability when it was taken over, and that gave it a revenue which enabled it, of course, to have a profit at once. That is the position, and that liability with respect to the note issue, transferred from the country to the bank, was made the subject matter of considerable criticism, because after that it took over the gold reserve, and thus it was said that a private institution had control of the gold reserve. That was remedied two years ago, and if the Minister of Finance will read his speech of that time he will see that he endeavoured to make me, and I think other members of the house, believe that this was the best possible method to effect the best and highest possible purpose in the best possible world.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: I believed so then and I believe so still; but I believe it is much more important that the national bank should have general national acceptance than that my opinion should be sustained.

speechtext: If the hon. gentleman believes it still, we have the amazing spectacle of his asking us to accept something which he himself thinks is second only to that which he did two years ago.

That is all I desire to say with respect to this matter at the moment, because I am going to deal with the question when the bill is before us. I notice that the resolution does not deal with that; obviously there is no necessity for it, but it does not deal
with the consequential amendments that will be necessary. It provides for the redemption of the shares, but it does not provide for the amendment of the act. subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC

I say that still. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext:
What was said, of course, can be looked up; it was a lengthy debate, and as yet I have not found it. My point is this, however, that to my mind it is more important that the people of Canada should be agreed that they have a national bank; much more important that they should cease controversy regarding its constitution, than it is that my beliefs as to the best constitution of a bank should be sustained. The government is hoping by this legislation to quiet any discussion or any divergence of view regarding the constitution of the bank and to confine discussion to what shall be done with the instrument, and I entirely approve what the right hon. gentleman has said with regard to the bank being an arm of government but not a department of government. It is of the greatest importance that the men who are operating this arm of government should be in the highest degree independent in the exercise of their judgment in the job of work they have to do. The general broad policy of the bank of course must be in harmony with the desires of a majority of this parliament. If it is not, then the government of the day, with the aid of its majority, can come to parliament and propose and carry
Bank of Canada

through such changes in the legislation as, in the view of the majority, may be desirable at the time; and to that extent what my right hon. friend said with respect to a government led by the hon. member for Lethbridge of course would be true. One -would expect that if the people of Canada sent to this parliament a majority of members who believed in the theories of the hon. member for Lethbridge and his followers, that majority would so amend this legislation as to bring it into line with those theories. That is democracy.
The machinery which this bill proposes to set up does not make rapid transition easy, it is true, because in the bill we are providing that the directors are to be appointed for a period of, speaking from memory, three years; but there would be nothing to prevent a government possessing a majority in this parliament from coming to parliament and amending even that provision of the law. There is no doubt about it; by this action, and indeed by the action we took in 1936, we do take the very great responsibility of initiating, as an arm of government, a national institution for the control of credit and currency under aegis of this parliament. We did that in 1936, and this does not change the fact in the slightest degree. It does endeavour to quiet controversy as to whether or not that was effectively done in 1936. I am of opinion that it was. Personally I believe it was done in a better way than the method provided by this bill; but I do believe it is much more desirable that my fellow countrymen should be satisfied with the constitution of a national bank than it is that my particular ideas should prevail as to the manner in which national control should be made effective.
That is why, as clearly as I can express it, I am explaining the introduction of the resolution now before the committee. I have no apologies to make, because I believe that by the control of currency and credit through this arm of government we are assuming a responsibility in this parliament in connection with which we must build up a tradition of non-partisan administration. My right hon. friend the leader of the opposition expressed his fears in regard to partisanship entering into appointments by a bank which was controlled by the government. Of course that danger exists, and it can be obviated only by high-minded men in the seat of government refusing to permit that to be done. For my part I say here in this house what I have said to scores of correspondents who have written me with respect to positions in the Bank of Canada: " I have nothing whatever to do [DOT] with appointments to the Bank of Canada.
tMr. Dunning.]
Under the law the management is responsible for such appointments. Communicate with the proper officials of the bank in the same manner that you would with respect to obtaining a position in any other business institution." There is nothing to compel a Minister of Finance to do that; but I am endeavouring, as I believe my right hon. friend was sincerely endeavouring, to follow that line in relation to the bank. The only hope we can have is that men will continue to follow it until such a tradition of non-interference in matters of that kind is built up that it will be difficult for anybody to break it, a tradition which in fact would enable a management of the bank properly to repudiate such interference, and successfully appeal to this parliament against it. That is all we can hope for along that line. I can only give the personal pledge that, so far as I am concerned, there will be absolutely no interference of that kind.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: May I say as a member of that proud group classed as monetary reformers, that we welcome the concession made by the Minister of Finance to-night in conceding that in money matters even the Minister of Finance, the Bank of Canada and the government of the nation should bow to the will of the people. I am amused at the concern expressed by the leader of the opposition as to whether or not the establishment of complete public ownership is going to make the Bank of Canada an effective arm of government. That was an issue I thought was very clearly and definitely settled during the campaign of 1935.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: I did not think this was going to make it an effective arm of government.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: I understood the right hon. gentleman to say that he was afraid it might make it that.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: Surely the hon. member's hearing is better than that.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: I must confess that I did not hear the right hon. gentleman very well, although on several occasions I asked him to speak up. Certainly I have no desire to misquote him.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: I did not say that. I said I hoped the effect of the legislation would be to make the bank an arm of government, and I agreed with what the minister had said and hoped that it would not become a department of government.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext:
To guarantee that the bank would have no chance of becoming a department of government, in 1934 the present leader

Bank of Canada
of the opposition enacted the Bank of Canada Act which established the bank as a purely private institution, free from the control of the government. And the issue which came up during the discussion of the Bank of Canada measure made very clear the distinction between the Conservative and Liberal policies on that all-Canadian public matter.
For instance, at that time the Hon. J. L. Ralston was Liberal financial critic, and in dealing with that very point he said:
The control of credit and currency is the biggest and most important public utility in the activities of the nation. There are certain things which should be under public ownership or public control, and the first and most important of these is the institution, the Bank of Canada, which controls, which guides and which directs the whole economic life of the nation.
There was no question as to the stand of the Hon, Mr. Ralston on that occasion. It was in direct conflict with the policy of private ownership which the government of that day had established. The then leader of the opposition, the Prime Minister of to-day (Mr. Mackenzie King) supported that conclusion with these statements:
Once a nation parts with its currency and credit, it matters not who makes the nation's laws. Usury once in control will wreck any nation. Until the control of the issue of currency and credit is restored to government, and recognized as its most conspicuous and sacred responsibility, all talk of the sovereignty of parliament is idle and futile.
These declarations by the Hon. Mr. Ralston .and the then right hon. the leader of the opposition were, first, that the control of currency and credit should be recognized as a public utility service, under the direct control of the government and, second, that it was a duty of the government, not a duty of private monopoly, to control the issue of currency and credit to be issued in terms of public need, not of private gain.
I am satisfied that this is a step towards the fulfilment of those promises, which were the promises upon which some of us won our elections, and which indicated that the policy of the Liberal party was that if returned to office it would establish our parliament as a Canadian democratic institution which would be superior to the private money system.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
