hon. member could not quote a word of mine to the contrary effect said anywhere at any time.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: What I want to say to the Minister of Finance is this, that the other day when I heard him deal with monetary reform I was wondering if he had in mind some of the statements made by the present Prime Minister, the head of the Liberal party, in the house in 1933 and 1934.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext:
It was his colleague, the
Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie).

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext:
Does he remember what
the Minister of National Defence had declared, as a financial reformer, in the Vancouver campaign during the election of 1935? The Minister of Finance was not in the house when that great debate took place. So far as I know, he was not in the heat of the campaign of 1935. Possibly monetary reform has not become an issue down in Prince Edward Island, the little province by the sea, which he represents in the house, and which is a long way away from the rigid, virile and active reformer group which first sent him to Ottawa.
I would say to the Minister of Finance that the great issue is this: Is the question of the control of the issue of currency and finance going to 'be advanced by this extensive use of Canadian moneys which are going to be used to purchase back at a profit a part of the concession which was made to the private money system by the Conservative government in 1934?
Later on, on the second reading of the bill I hope to expose the details of the concession as the most iniquitous concession passed, or approved by a Canadian parliament since confederation. I am quite aware of the declaration that the Bank of Canada has control over the issue of currency and credit, and1 I shall deal with that issue to-night. To make the matter clear, I wish to make the state-
Bank of Canada

ment, first, and then prove it, that under the present practice neither the government of Canada nor the Bank of Canada exercises a single bit of control over the volume or currency or credit that is placed in circulation by the country through the chartered banks, who are the only ones that can put currency and credit into circulation.
To deal with that subject, I want first to take some statements made to the house by the Minister of Finance, which are in accord with the public statements made by the governor of the Bank of Canada to the people of Canada. The address of March 8, delivered by the present Minister of Finance, is now in circulation as an address on monetary policy. At page 1 of that pamphlet his words are as follows:
Parliament has set up an institution, now controlled by the government, charged with the specific duty of regulating the volume of currency and credit in the best interests of the economic life of the nation.
That is a broad statement. It indicates that through the Bank of Canada we are serving the economic life of the nation by controlling and regulating the issue of currency.
Again on page 4 that declaration is amplified by this statement:
Recognizing that the regulation of the country's credit and currency was so vital a sovereign function that it could not be left in the control of a private institution, this government in 1936 amended the Bank of Canada Act to give the dominion government effective control over the hank by majority ownership of the capital stock and majority control of the board of directors.
Effective control over the Bank of Canada does not necessarily mean effective control over the chartered banks, which are responsible for the issue of currency and credit.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: They are not solely responsible for currency.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext:
No, but the thing that we issue to-day as a medium of exchange for both government and people is not Bank of Canada bills for out-of-pocket transactions, but as the leader of the opposition knows, bank deposits, controlled by cheques. That is what our banks are using to-day to purchase government interest-bearing bonds, and I want to deal with that a little later.
At the end of that statement the right hon. leader of the opposition is quoted as stating, "No wonder you laugh," and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) replied, "I cheer." I am quite satisfied of this, that there are many of us on this side of the house and elsewhere throughout the dominion who would gladly swell the chorus of cheers of the Minister of Justice if we believed, as he believes.
fMr. McGeer.]
that through the machinery presently existing, the Bank of Canada, we -were in control of the currency and credit of the nation. But I for one do not see any reason to cheer yet, even with the complete ownership of all the stock of the Bank of Canada, although I think that is a step in the right direction. I want to give my reasons for that, and I hope my remarks will not be taken in a sense other than that I wish to contribute to the fulfilment of the great promises which were made to the people of Canada by the Liberal party, upon which I believe they were elected, and through which I believe we can find a way to make a better, greater, bigger and happier Dominion of Canada.
In showing how the alleged public control of currency and credit is operated in the best interests of the economic life of the nation, the Minister of Finance gave this considered explanation:
The Bank of Canada exercises its control over the chartered banks by operating on the cash reserves of the banking system, either by conducting so-called open market operations or by altering its rediscount rate, or by both.
And then he added:
These are the major weapons which the central bank may use in carrying out its primary function of controlling the volume of credit and currency in use in the country.
Those are the two major weapons, and I propose to bring to the attention of the committee that neither one of those weapons is available as a medium of the exercise of one bit of power either by government or by the Bank of Canada.
During the course of his address the following interesting exchange took place between the Minister of Finance and the right hon. leader of the opposition:
Mr. Dunning: The second well known mechanism by which the central bank exercises control is the deliberate raising or lowering of its rediscount rate. High rates, of course, tend to contract business enterprise, and low rates tend towards expansion.
Mr. Bennett:	But there are no rediscounts
in Canada.
Mr. Dunning: The rediscount rate is in effect; I shall come to that in a moment.
But the Minister of Finance never did deal in that address with the issue which the leader of the opposition raised, namely, that although we have a rediscount rate there are no rediscounts in Canada.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: There was only one since we were established as a bank.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext:
The right hon. gentleman knows just as well as I do that the redis-

Bank oj Canada
count rate went out when England set up a managed currency system, and that was all abandoned.
We are told in this house that it is one of the major weapons through which we have fulfilled the promises that were made by our government in 1935, and upon which we were elected, to create a new condition for the circulation of currency and credit to serve the economic life of this nation. I wonder if the Prime Minister, the members of the government and the members of this house are aware that our chartered banks are not borrowers and do not borrow legal tender cash from the Bank of Canada. Consequently the rate of interest fixed by the bank, that is the rediscount rate, has no bearing on the credit policy of our Canadian chartered banks. The reason why our chartered banks do not borrow Bank of Canada bills is that the Bank of Canada by purchasing gold and other securities has supplied the chartered banks with more Bank of Canada bills free of any interest charge or other charge whatever than they need to hold as legal reserves to support the bank deposits they have on issue. As a matter of fact, under section 59, subsection 4 of our Bank Act, our chartered banks are now privileged to take a five dollar Bank of Canada bill and to exchange on the security of that five dollars, $100 of bank deposits written into the bank's books by a mere stroke of the pen, for either a one hundred dollar treasury bill or a one hundred dollar interest-bearing bond. That was the concession which was made to the chartered banks by the government of 1934, and they are not missing the opportunity; for to-day they hold $1,155,000,000 of such securities, an increase of $471,000,000 since that great concession was made when the Bank Act was amended to reduce gold reserves to twenty-five per cent and to reduce cash reserves to five per cent. To-day the chartered banks of Canada-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC

please distinguish between the chartered banks and the national bank?

I say the chartered banks hold legal tender currency, which they own outright, for which they pay nothing, which they have secured freer than they used to secure the right to print their own currency, because the cost of printing them is now borne by the Bank of Canada, to a total, according to the May report of the Bank of Canada, of $247,000,000, $199,000,000 of which is on deposit with the bank and the balance is held in the bankers' tills. That is over and above the $102,000,000 which the
Bank of Canada has on issue and in circulation with the public. What does that mean? Without borrowing a single dollar from the Bank of Canada, the chartered banks can secure $2,800,000,000 of bank deposits, and with their surplus reserves, which are to-day idle and unemployed, they can increase those bank deposits to $4,800,000,000. How preposterous then to say that the bank rate policy, which includes a change in the rediscount rate, is one of the major weapons by which we control, through the Bank of Canada, the issue of currency and credit in this nation, when that part of the bank rate policy has no operation upon the existing deposits or upon the $2,000,000,000 of deposits which our chartered banks may use! I want to say this:
I cannot blame the Minister of Finance for that technical explanation, but I am satisfied that somebody in his department was responsible for it.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: I believe there is.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext:
Well then, it cannot be
through the bank rate. It must be, then, through the other major weapon, open market operations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: That is it.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance
agrees to that proposition. Now I want to show the committee that the open market operation is even more innocuous and less a factor in the control over currency and credit issue than is the bank rate policy. Let me point out that the Bank of Canada has issued through the open market operation, that is in the open purchase of gold and other securities, a sufficient amount of Bank of Canada bills to give the chartered banks $103,000,000 outright, which they own outright in excess of the reserves required for the bank deposits they have on record. The Minister of Finance went on to deal with that. But before I proceed to deal with the open market operation, I want to draw the attention of the Prime Minister to the fact that one of the results of the open market operation has been to give the chartered banks, free of charge, a sufficient amount of Bank of Canada cash to release them from the controlling influence of any change in the rediscount rate by the Bank of Canada. The result of this is that one of the major weapons which the Bank of Canada employs, according to the statement of the Minister of Finance, namely the change in the rediscount rate, to regulate the volume of currency and credit in use in the country, is destroyed by one branch of the open market operation, namely the purchasing of securities on the open market with Bank of Canada bills.
If the rediscount picture is out of the picture, let us deal with this open market operation. Let us for the purpose of practical illustration assume that the Bank of Canada went into the market and bought $10,000,000 worth of securities and that the $10,000,000 were put into circulation as we were told by the Minister of Finance, though unfortunately, no matter from whom the purchase is made, the money would find its way into the chartered banks' tills. What would the chartered banks do with that $10,000,000? Would they, as he suggests, increase their bank deposits by making new purchases and new loans to the value of $100,000,000? They would not do any such thing. They would (Mr. McGeer.]	[DOT]
do exactly what they are doing now; they would increase their reserves of $103,000,000 by $10,000,000, and the amount of currency and credit in circulation in the country would not be affected by a single dollar. Of course my hon. friend says, "Oh, but the banks would be very foolish to have $10,000,000 of Bank of Canada bills that they could use as reserves of bank deposits of ten times that amount, without using them." But what I want to point out to this committee is that they are already doing that very thing, according to the May report, with $103,000,000. To talk about controlling the issue of currency and credit, in the face of that fact, by either the rediscount rate or the purchase of securities, is to state something that the facts of the Bank of Canada report disclose is contrary to actual banking practice in the Dominion of Canada to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: Oh, that is awful.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext:
My hon. friend shakes
his head. Well, I may be wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: I gave figures.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext:
But what I am placing
before the committee is an argument based on facts, not on theories.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: I gave figures of the expansion.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext:
Oh, yes, but that did not
have anything to do with expansion, surplus Bank of Canada reserves.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: Oh, yes, it did.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: What I say is this, that to-day the Bank of Canada has idle, unemployed and being hoarded on deposit with the Bank of Canada, $103,000,000. Yet we are told that another issue of $10,000,000 will affect the volume of currency and credit not available for loans but in circulation serving the economic life of the nation. It cannot serve it while it is being hoarded by our chartered banks.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: They get no interest, you know.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: They do not even pay for the printing of the bills. Yet my hon. friend says that they do not pay any interest. I have been a little suspicious that we as a Liberal party and as a nation have been suffering from the very monetary policy which the people of Canada overwhelmingly repudiated in 1935. The rediscount rate is out; the open market operation by buying is out; let us see what would happen if-did the minister speak?

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has certainly disposed of it. He says it is out.

Bank of Canada

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext:
I never hope to convince the Minister of National Revenue, but I am .submitting that the facts I have offered to the committee should, to one of ordinary intelligence, indicate that they are valid. It may be that this is not the idea of the Minister of National Revenue, and he has just as much right to his opinions as I have to mine. But I want to say to him, with due deference to his present position of authority, that I have given this problem a great many more hours of thought and study than he has given it.	,
Let me now deal with the other factor. We are told that if the Bank of Canada went on the market to sell securities-what would happen? The assumption is that the Bank of Canada, by selling securities, would have payments for them in its own legal tender cash, namely Bank of Canada bills. Therefore there would be withdrawn from circulation, first, the Bank of Canada reserves that are in excess of reserves legally required to support existing deposits amounting to $103,000,000. But what would be the result if the Bank of Canada continued to sell securities after those reserves were exhausted? Then the Bank of Canada would have to take from the chartered banks the amounts required legally to sustain existing bank deposits. That would compel the Bank of Canada and the chartered banks to withdraw loans now in circulation. What would be the result of that? It would be *disastrously to precipitate the present recession into a major depression. If I am right [DOT]on the figures as I have interpreted them, which I have taken from the Bank of Canada report, this elaborate control that the Minister of Finance so clearly outlined to us means nothing under the rediscount rate, means nothing under the sale of securities, and only means that there is left to the Bank of Canada power to precipitate a disastrous and appalling, not recession, but depression of the worst kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: To control overexpansion, the power is there.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext:
Well, I cannot agree with that, because I suggest that the facts do not support it. You could withdraw, of course; there is no doubt about that. One of the great lessons in monetary reform, which the Macmillan committee taught the British parliament and upon which the British parliament has acted, was that the rediscount rate, the bank rate policy, was only effective in precipitating a depression and not effective in restoring prosperity or maintaining stability. What has been abandoned in England since the British Empire currency policy of 1933 was adopted-and we adopted it in this house -the rediscount rate and the open market
policy, is recognized as being a minor, inferior and ineffective method of control; and direct control by the government is recognized as the only policy available. It is quite true that they have not taken over the Bank of England, quite true that they have not taken over the chartered banks. But I listened to the present Prime Minister of England and to the governor of the Bank of England, and I heard the governor of the Bank of England declare:
We are glad as bankers, and I speak for the Bank of England and for the bankers of England, for the measure of freedom which we enjoy in this country. We shall exercise that freedom in the only proper way that we can, and that is in support of the government; and if the government through the proper channels will make known to us its policies and what they wish us to do in augmenting those policies, we will in good will and loyalty comply with those requests, as though we were compelled so to do.
There is not a policy of legal domination; but I am satisfied that if the banks of England failed to cooperate with the government in the prosecution of its policies, nationalization would follow without delay, because I am sure that to-day in England neither the House of Commons nor-whatever may have been its constitution in the past-the House of Lords is controlled by the gold mongers and debt dealers of Lombard street. They have made the monetary system in England the servant of the British government and the British people, and the bankers in acquiescing are now finding that government directed policy and a new reconstructive program, with cooperation between the banks and the government, are infinitely better, even for the banks, than the more restricted policy of their own design.
The Macmillan report, if it is read correctly, was a major report looking to international trade recovery through international cooperation. But if international recovery and cooperation did not come, then it looked to government spending and government control, with a managed currency system. They said that it was not possible or indeed practical to regard our monetary system as an automatic system grinding out the right result by the operation of some well-worn rules of thumb. We were told by the Minister of Finance that the major weapons of the central bank to control the volume of credit and currency in the country are the rediscount rate and the open market operations. Well, the automatic system, whereby the chartered banks were supposed to create and issue, and circulate or withdraw bank deposit money according to changes in the volume of Bank of Canada bills issued, was abandoned. They found it would
Bank oj Canada

not work, and the automatic system gave way to what is now recognized-the Minister of Finance himself admitted it-as a managed paper standard in which the value of the currency is not maintained and stabilized by convertibility into gold but is maintained by management on a basis of supplying the demand which the progress of the nation asserts.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: Which is exactly what we are doing to-day.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: Then why is this nation embarrassed for want of money in every department of government?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: It is not.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: Yes, in the provincial governments and municipalities as well. Why have a confiscatory taxation system? Why can we not build highways to serve the tourist trade? Why can we not get on with the rehabilitation of the railways? "No money" is the cry everywhere.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: My hon. friend quotes England. Will he tell us what England is doing with respect to that matter? He quotes England one minute and then comes back to me.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: Let me tell the Minister of Finance this. During the last five years England has spent $5,000,000,000 on battleships and guns, and in addition to that huge expenditure she carries her line of communication from the heart of the empire down through the Atlantic, past Gibraltar, through the Mediterranean into Palestine and Egypt and into almost every part of Europe, on through the Red sea and across India to her great base at Singapore and on to Australia and New Zealand.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: That is not answering my question.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: She is carrying that load of responsibility and carrying it successfully. Well, then, let me ask the Minister of Finance this question: If England can invest $5,000,000,000 in battleships and guns which can never return a dollar of profit, why cannot we invest a few hundred millions to put unemployed Canadians to work building highways which will return the greatest profit in any department of trade that we can develop? The Minister of Finance says that I quote what England has done. Well, England pays the entire bill for unemployment relief. England pays the entire cost of health insurance and much of the health service.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: By taxation.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext:
Not by taxation. She
balanced her budget this year by borrowing over $623,000,000. The situation in England is much different from ours. England must import food; she must import the means of shelter; she must import materials for industry; she must import materials for armaments; she must buy her gold abroad. In Canada we produce all these things, far in excess of our own needs, with an exportable surplus that gave us a favourable balance of trade of $627,000,000 according to the budget speech.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: No, no.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: How much was it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: Balance of payments.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: Well, I think that included tourist trade and physical trade and sale of gold, making up $627,000,000. But whether it was balance of payments or balance of trade does not make much difference; it was a gross international trade, gross revenue bigger than our total national expenditure. Yet England, facing an unfavourable trade balance, an unfavourable balance of payments-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: No.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance
says, "Hear, hear," but we were told that that was one of the major weapons of control by which we regulate the volume of credit and currency in the country. As I have pointed out, that is the only power you have under your present system of control. I commend that section to hon. members to read for themselves; they ought to be able to read it as well as myself. The section goes on:
Moreover, those who are in charge of our monetary system will, naturally and excusably, be reluctant to carry through so ruthless a policy to its proper conclusion, with the result that we may continue for a long period in a depressed condition with severe losses and severe unemployment and yet with not enough of both to compel by fprce majeure the necessary readjustments of incomes.
Moreover, once such a condition of depression has become firmly established, a policy of dear money will no longer be necessary to ensure its continuance for it will contain within itself the seed of its own perpetuation.
What was the alternative suggestion as to the control that should be exercised? If hon. members will go through the report, they will find at page 136, section 316, this statement: The decline of new enterprise has reacted adversely on profit and prices, and the low level of profits and prices stands in the way of new enterprise.
It is for that reason that some of us think that in the domestic field it may be necessary to invoke governmental enterprise to break the vicious circle.
What is the governmental enterprise that has been invoked in England? Expenditure on
social services, a great program of aid to housing, a new program of swelling national defences, a vast program of aid in the rehabilitation of industry, and a thousand channels, even including cooperation with the governments of Canada and New Zealand to subsidize a Pacific ocean service; in all these ways, not by one or two things such as a housing program or a little contribution to municipalities, but in a hundred ways the government has taken control of the monetary system and is putting consumers' buying power into circulation not merely in the form of aid to those in need but as a means of sustaining the economic blood stream of industry and commerce of the capitalistic system that the government of England is charged to sustain, as we as a Liberal party are charged to sustain the industry and commerce of a capitalistic Canada. I say to the government and to hon. members that if we fail to fulfil that sovereign obligation of government, we shall have failed our country at a time when England, after years of experience, has shown the way.
I do not want to be critical. I quite appreciate that in a house consisting of 245 members no man can make any contribution who does not command some respect from his fellow members. I do not want to speak as a crank or one who thinks there is efficacy only in more spending of money. I have no faith whatever in the theories of the social credit party, because I am convinced' that the operation of that program would do infinitely more social harm than economic good. In 1934 the Liberal party in this house declared that the control, issue and circulation of the currency and credit of this nation were the most conspicuous and sacred responsibility of government, and that in the exercise of that control the government alone could demonstrate that parliament was sovereign. I believe this parliament is taking a great step forward in the economic history of this nation. The ownership of the Bank of Canada is only a step; the establishment of a policy that will fulfil the terms of that ownership is the next step; but there is no retreating from that step once it is taken. This is the first step in the emancipation of Canadian democracy from the slavery of orthodox finance, a system that has given us the experience of seeing every contribution of science to progress stalemated and set back by what? By a constant increase in our mountain of unpayable, interest-bearing debt.
No man in parliament, no government, no responsible authority should ever disdain the experiences of history. I am free to confess that in monetary history there are many
Bank of Canada

pages which indicate that the greatest caution must be exercised in the management of a currency to serve a nation. But we are not starting blindly when we follow the lead of England; and by now, after seven years of depression, with riots in our peaceful cities because men claim, whether rightly or wrongly, that they have a desire to go to work, we should know what we are doing. We have jobs in. Nova Scotia crying to be done. Why, the highways down in that province. Mr. Chairman, are not built for the cars we are driving to-day, capable of eighty miles an hour. They are built for the horse and buggy or the model T Ford. We have even worse roads in British Columbia. It does not matter where you go in this dominion; there is no national highway system, and that is one of the things in which you can invest successfully. No method of increasing the volume of international revenue offers greater opportunities than the development of a real highway system in the Dominion of Canada. I wonder if we are not amazed to see the premier of my own province going to Washington in connection with the construction of a highway through to Alaska. What will he get with which to build that highway? He will get printing-press dollars, printed by the United States government, that are not backed by any gold reserve; because neither bank deposits nor the printing press currency of the United States can now be converted into gold in that country.
It is all very well to go back to the old story "Why, that would be inflation." On the second reading of this bill I hope to place before the house the results of the inflation established as a possibility on the part of the chartered banks, but I do commend to the Prime Minister and his government serious and fair consideration of my statement to-night that the major weapons of control, by which we were told the government through the Bank of Canada would regulate the volume of currency and credit in the interests of the economic life of the nation, are not effective; because I am satisfied that the majority of the members of the government will not permit that statement to go unchallenged, if my conclusions, from the facts I have analysed to-night, are justified and correct.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext:
I have listened with a great deal of interest to the splendid address delivered by the hon. gentleman who has just spoken. He states that he has no faith in social credit, but I find it difficult to see any difference between the proposals he has given the committee and the principles enunciated by social credit. With him we ask the govern-
ment to fulfil their pre-election promises. We believe that the ownership of the Bank of Canada, though a step in the right direction, is not sufficient. We listened to the Minister of Finance tell us that the government had established complete control of the issue of money and credit, and we expected that the policy of the bank would be such that money and credit would be issued in terms of public need.
To give a simple illustration of what I mean by issuing credit in terms of public need, I say to the minister that we can and do. produce in Canada hundreds of thousands of gallons of milk, more milk than we can possibly consume in this country. On the other hand, throughout the land there are thousands of little children who, these hot summer days, want an ice-cream cone; but because they have not that little round disc that we call a nickel, that has very little actual money value as far as the metal in it is concerned, they cannot have that cone. All we ask is that the children of this country be allowed to have the nickels that are necessary to purchase the ice-cream that we can produce in such large quantities.
As another illustration, I might point to the number of people in this land and in the United States who own motor cars and who desire to visit different parts of this country. They would do so if our highways were greatly improved. There are thousands and thousands of men willing to work on the highways; there are great deposits from which we can manufacture the cement required, and there are plenty of gravel and sand pits available. There is no shortage of material; the only thing we lack is the money or credit with which to pay these men for their contribution towards the development of Canadian highways.
I could cite illustration after illustration to show that the needs of the people of Canada are not being satisfied; with regard to health and education; the needs of municipalities in connection with providing services to the people; the needs of the provincial governments in connection with social services, and so on. We believe that the government should advise the experts, who, the minister says, will staff the bank, so to regulate our monetary system that it will actually reflect our collective ability to produce goods and services in this country.
As reported at page 3903 of Hansard the Minister of Finance is reported to have said:
There are some, of course, who appear to believe that the government should not pay interest at all or, indeed-

Bank of Canada

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: May I respectfully call the attention of the chair to the fact that the hon. member is now entering upon the budget debate. He is now quoting from my budget speech. Under the rules of the house that speech would come before the house in the budget debate, and I submit the hon. member cannot anticipate that debate on this discussion.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: In my opinion the point of order is well taken.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: Then I shall not read it. I simply wished to refer to the statement of monetary policy, and the reference made by the minister to monetary reform in general.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: There will be plenty of opportunity in the debate on the budget.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext: So far as the point of order is concerned, there is no reason why he should not read it at this time.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OP THE PUBLIC
speechtext:
The minister's remarks with respect to monetary reformers was to the effect that he was not going to issue money and credit debt free. He was not going to use the Bank of Canada, or any facilities he might have, to create money to be used to lower the debts of Canada.
Some time ago I asked the government if they had any plan which, if pursued, would pay off Canada's national debt in a period of twenty years, thirty years, or fifty years. The minister answered that it was a matter of government policy, and that he would not answer the question. But that question must be answered. It is a hoary fallacy to believe that we can borrow ourselves out of debt, or tax ourselves to prosperity. The municipal debts of this country are rising at a tremendous rate. Over 81,400,000,000 is owed by the municipalities. The provincial debt is increasing at an alarming rate, and has now reached a total of over $1,700,000,000; the national debt of Canada is over $3,000,000,000, and that amount has been added to in the last fiscal year. In the past we have financed through this debt creating system. The only prosperity we have ever enjoyed in Canada has been during a period when the greatest volume of private and public debt was amassed, and at a time when municipal, provincial and federal governments were spending large sums of money. Under that debt creating system we have a period of prosperity; but once that credit is restricted, and once we have reached the saturation point so far as borrowing is concerned, we have arrived at a critical situation.
To-day many municipalities are bankrupt, and many provincial governments are facing bankruptcy. The federal government claims to have complete control over the issue of money and credit, and I suggest that it provide municipal and provincial governments with debt free money, or at least make provision for lowering private and public debts. We are going to watch with a great deal of interest the policy pursued by the experts who will be staffing the Bank of Canada. Once more I will say that this is a step in the right direction, and we are pleased the government has seen fit to take over the complete ownership of the Bank of Canada. We now await the fulfilment of the promises made by the Liberal party. There might be a difference of opinion as to the methods to be adopted. The suggestions by the social credit group might not be accepted by the Liberal party; but there can be no difference of opinion on the fact that the purchasing power of the people must be raised if we are going to be able to raise the standard of living.
